lead: An inverter turns DC into AC by switching a load between DC rails. In square-wave operation each switch is on for half the output period, so the load sees a rectangular voltage whose height is fixed by the DC bus and whose frequency is set by the switching rate. The half-bridge uses two switches and a split capacitor bus; the full bridge (H-bridge) uses four switches and gives twice the voltage. Every PWM method later in this unit runs on the same bridge.
prereq: You need: the IGBT and its anti-parallel diode (see Power BJT, MOSFET and IGBT) and the Fourier series of a square wave.

blocks.text: The half-bridge has two switches, S1 on top and S2 below, in series across the DC bus V<sub>dc</sub>. Two equal capacitors C1 and C2 are also in series across the bus, so their junction O sits at half the bus voltage. The load is connected between the switch midpoint A and the capacitor midpoint O. Taking O as the reference, the top rail is at +V<sub>dc</sub>/2 and the bottom rail at −V<sub>dc</sub>/2.

With S1 on, v<sub>AO</sub> = +V<sub>dc</sub>/2; with S2 on, v<sub>AO</sub> = −V<sub>dc</sub>/2. Each switch is gated for 180° of the output cycle, so the load voltage is a square wave of height V<sub>dc</sub>/2. Its rms is also V<sub>dc</sub>/2, since v² never changes.
vo = Σ (2Vdc/nπ) sin nωt, n = 1, 3, 5, … ω = 2πf is the output angular frequency and n the harmonic order. The fundamental peak is 2Vdc/π = 0.637Vdc (rms 0.45Vdc).

The capacitors must be large enough that O does not move while they carry the load current. Each switch still blocks the whole bus V<sub>dc</sub> when off. Some syllabi call this the split-supply inverter.

sections.h3: Full bridge: four switches, twice the voltage

blocks.text: The full bridge has two legs: S1 over S2 (leg A) and S3 over S4 (leg B), with the load between the midpoints A and B. The diagonal pairs are gated in turn, and the two switches of one leg are never on together.
vo = Σ (4Vdc/nπ) sin nωt, n = 1, 3, 5, … The fundamental peak is 4Vdc/π = 1.273Vdc (rms 0.9Vdc); the nth harmonic is 1/n of it.

Even harmonics and DC are absent because the wave has half-wave symmetry, v(t + T/2) = −v(t). The rms of the whole wave is V<sub>dc</sub>, so the total harmonic distortion is THD = √(V<sub>rms</sub>² − V<sub>1</sub>²)/V<sub>1</sub> = √(1 − 0.9²)/0.9 = 48.3 %, whatever V<sub>dc</sub> is. The full bridge gives twice the half-bridge voltage from the same bus and switch rating.

sections.h3: R-L load and the feedback diodes

blocks.text: With an R-L load the current cannot reverse at the instant the voltage does. In steady state it rises exponentially towards +V<sub>dc</sub>/R in the positive half cycle and falls towards −V<sub>dc</sub>/R in the negative half, with time constant τ = L/R, swinging between −I<sub>max</sub> and +I<sub>max</sub>.
Imax = (Vdc/R)·tanh(T/4τ) T is the output period in seconds and τ = L/R in seconds.

Follow one half cycle. At t = 0 the gates move from S2, S3 to S1, S4, but the current is still −I<sub>max</sub>. S1 and S4 cannot carry negative current, so it flows through their anti-parallel diodes D1 and D4 into the positive rail, returning the inductor's energy to the source. Only when the current passes zero, at t<sub>x</sub> = τ ln(1 + tanh(T/4τ)), do S1 and S4 take over. These are the feedback diodes.

Harmonic by harmonic, I<sub>n</sub> = V<sub>n</sub>/|Z<sub>n</sub>| with |Z<sub>n</sub>| = √(R² + (nωL)²). |Z<sub>n</sub>| grows with n, so the current is much closer to a sine than the voltage, and I<sub>rms</sub> = √(I<sub>1</sub>² + I<sub>3</sub>² + I<sub>5</sub>² + …).

If both switches of one leg are on together the bus is shorted: this is shoot-through. The gate pattern turns the outgoing switch off and waits a dead time of 1 to 3 μs before turning the incoming one on; a diode carries the load current in the gap. Dead time slightly lowers the fundamental and adds low-order distortion.

items: Peak blocking voltage of each switch: V<sub>dc</sub>, in both bridges.
Peak switch current: the peak load current (V<sub>dc</sub>/R for a resistor, I<sub>max</sub> for R-L); with a resistor the average is half of it.
To change the output voltage without changing Vdc, the switching pattern must change: see single and multiple pulse modulation.

figure.caption: The second worked example: a 220 V full bridge feeding 10 Ω and 25 mH at 50 Hz. The load voltage is a ±220 V square wave; the current swings exponentially between −21.2 A and +21.2 A, and for the first 1.69 ms after each switching it flows back to the source through the diodes.

spec.aria: A full-bridge circuit: a 220 volt source, switches S1 to S4 each with an anti-parallel diode, and a 10 ohm, 25 millihenry load between midpoints A and B. Below, the load voltage is a plus and minus 220 volt square wave and the load current an exponential wave between minus and plus 21.2 amperes; the first 1.69 milliseconds of each half cycle are shaded as diode conduction.

examples.question: A single-phase full bridge runs from V<sub>dc</sub> = 300 V and feeds a 20 Ω resistor at 50 Hz in square-wave mode. Find (a) the rms output, (b) the power, (c) the rms fundamental and its power, (d) the rms third harmonic, (e) the THD and (f) the peak and average switch current.
steps: (a) V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>dc</sub> = 300 V, because v² = 300² at every instant.
(f) Peak current = V<sub>dc</sub>/R = 300/20 = 15 A. Each switch carries it for half the period, so its average is 7.5 A.
examples.answer: V<sub>rms</sub> = 300 V, P = 4500 W, V<sub>1</sub> = 270.09 V carrying 3647.6 W, V<sub>3</sub> = 90.03 V, THD = 48.3 %, switch current 15 A peak and 7.5 A average.

examples.question: A full bridge with V<sub>dc</sub> = 220 V feeds R = 10 Ω in series with L = 25 mH at 50 Hz in square-wave mode. Find (a) the peak load current, (b) how long the feedback diodes conduct after each switching, (c) the rms current from the first four harmonics and (d) the power and average supply current.
steps: (c) ωL = 2π × 50 × 0.025 = 7.854 Ω; V<sub>n</sub> = 4V<sub>dc</sub>/(nπ√2) and I<sub>n</sub> = V<sub>n</sub>/√(R² + (nωL)²):
I<sub>rms</sub> ≈ √(15.577² + 2.579² + 0.978² + 0.506²) = 15.83 A. Integrating the exponential current itself gives 15.83 A.
(d) Only R takes power: P = I<sub>rms</sub>² R = 15.83² × 10 = 2507 W. The average supply current is P/V<sub>dc</sub> = 2507/220 = 11.40 A.
examples.answer: I<sub>max</sub> = 21.21 A; the feedback diodes conduct for 1.69 ms after each switching; I<sub>rms</sub> ≈ 15.83 A; P ≈ 2507 W and the average supply current is 11.40 A.

traps: The half-bridge output is V<sub>dc</sub>/2 high (rms V<sub>dc</sub>/2); the full bridge gives V<sub>dc</sub>. Each switch blocks the full V<sub>dc</sub> in both.

The fundamental peak is 4V<sub>dc</sub>/π (full bridge) or 2V<sub>dc</sub>/π (half-bridge), not V<sub>dc</sub>; its rms is 0.9V<sub>dc</sub> or 0.45V<sub>dc</sub>. The nth harmonic is 1/n of the fundamental, not 1/n².
With an R-L load the voltage is still a square wave but the current is exponential, and the diodes, not the switches, conduct just after each switching.
120° conduction belongs to the three-phase bridge; a single-phase square-wave bridge gates each switch for 180°.

quiz.q: A half-bridge runs from a bus V<sub>dc</sub>. What is the height of its output square wave measured from zero, and what is the rms output?
quiz.a: The output swings between +V<sub>dc</sub>/2 and −V<sub>dc</sub>/2, so the height is V<sub>dc</sub>/2 and the rms is also V<sub>dc</sub>/2. The fundamental peak is 2V<sub>dc</sub>/π.

quiz.q: Why does the full-bridge square wave have no even harmonics?
quiz.a: It has half-wave symmetry, v(t + T/2) = −v(t); an even harmonic has the same sign half a period later, so its two halves cancel.

quiz.q: A full bridge has V<sub>dc</sub> = 200 V and R = 10 Ω. Find the rms fundamental voltage and the power it delivers.
Why are anti-parallel diodes needed with an R-L load even when the switches are IGBTs?
quiz.a: At each switching the inductor current still flows the old way; the incoming switches cannot carry it, so the diodes return it to the bus until it passes zero. Without them the L di/dt spike would destroy the switches.

quiz.q: In the R-L example, what happens to the diode conduction time if L is made larger, other values unchanged?
quiz.a: It rises. For L = 50 mH, τ = 5 ms and t<sub>x</sub> = 5 × ln(1 + tanh 1) = 5 × ln 1.762 = 2.83 ms, against 1.69 ms: more energy circulates back to the bus.

quiz.q: What is shoot-through and how is it prevented?
quiz.a: Both switches of one leg conduct and short the bus. A dead time is inserted between turning one off and the other on.

beyond: Not for the exam. Commercial inverters add a current loop, dead-time compensation and an LC filter so the output approaches a sine. SiC and GaN switches allow tens of kilohertz with small filters. Search for dead-time distortion and SiC half-bridge modules.
